what_its_for: Thioguanine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of leukemia (blood cancer), including acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It works by slowing or stopping the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_to_take: Take thioguanine by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Wash your hands thoroughly before and after handling this medicine. If a tablet is broken or crushed, avoid touching it with bare hands — use gloves if possible. Do not crush or chew the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight or body surface area (height and weight together). A common starting dose is about 2 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, but your dose may be different. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions. Do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine on your own, even if you feel well or feel sick.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at once or double up to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist right away.
storage: Store thioguanine tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in a dry place, away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist about the safest way to dispose of any unused or expired tablets — do not flush them down the toilet or throw them in regular household trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child while taking this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for some time after stopping — ask your doctor how long. Do not breastfeed while taking thioguanine. Avoid live vaccines (such as the flu nasal spray or chickenpox vaccine) while on this medicine without checking with your doctor first. Avoid close contact with people who have infections, as this medicine can weaken your immune system. Limit alcohol, as it may add to liver stress. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements, especially allopurinol (a gout medicine), as it can raise thioguanine levels in your blood and increase side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), severe stomach or belly pain, unusual swelling of your belly, dark urine or pale stools (signs of liver problems), unusual bleeding or bruising, black or bloody stools, signs of serious infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or severe sore throat, mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink, extreme tiredness or weakness, shortness of breath, or any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Thioguanine starts working at the cellular level right away, but it may take several weeks before you or your doctor see changes in your blood counts or cancer. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to monitor how the medicine is working and to watch for side effects. Be patient and keep all of your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Do not use during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Children: Thioguanine is used in children with leukemia, but doses are carefully calculated by weight. Follow your child's doctor's instructions exactly. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as low blood counts or liver problems. Close monitoring is important. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Genetic testing (TPMT enzyme): Some people have a genetic condition that makes them break down this medicine more slowly, which raises the risk of serious side effects. Your doctor may test for this before starting treatment.
